blockers.location: ch01/seat-cold/Deep read vs. Quiz Q4 / Card 4
blockers.message: Deep read identifies Abiah as Josiah's wife and Franklin's mother, but Quiz Q4's keyed answer and Card 4 both describe Abiah as one of the seventeen children ('the tenth by the second wife'), contradicting her identity as the second wife herself.

Full read is positioned as the deepest, most complete layer but never restates the Peter Folger / Cotton Mather material introduced in Deep read, even though Quiz Q9 tests that material. A reader relying on Full read alone as the standalone 'fullest' account cannot answer Q9 from it.

Example 6 asserts Franklin personally verified the uncle-Thomas birth coincidence against a parish register, an action the base chapter never attributes to him. The Full read instead presents the fact plainly and attributes the resemblance observation to people who 'later remarked' - the passive, reported framing that Example 6 explicitly claims Franklin did NOT rely on.

Card 4 describes Abiah as 'the tenth by the second wife,' treating her as one of the seventeen children, directly contradicting the Deep read's plain statement that Abiah was Franklin's mother (i.e., the second wife herself, not a child born to that marriage).

The question stem itself identifies Abiah as 'his second wife,' but the apparent intended-correct option c counts her among 'ten more by the second, including Abiah,' contradicting the stem within the same quiz item.

The Deep read references 'the Assembly's order' pushing the paper into Benjamin's name as if the reader already knows what that order was and why it happened, but Deep read never itself explains that James was jailed or why — that backstory only appears in Fast read (earlier) and is fully explained in Full read (later). A reader who consults only the Deep read layer, which is supposed to stand alone, hits an unexplained reference.

blockers.location: ch03/seat-skeptic/Newcastle letter (deep read vs. Example 5 / Implementation plan)
blockers.message: The chapter contradicts itself about who was physically at Newcastle. Deep read and other sections say Holmes tracked/traced FRANKLIN to or at Newcastle, but Example 5 and the Implementation plan both state Holmes himself 'wrote from Newcastle,' implying Holmes was the one there.

In back-to-back sentences, the Fast Read lists the copper coin as currently 'to his name' upon stepping off the boat, then says that same coin had already been paid away — leaving a reader unable to tell, from this standalone section, whether Franklin still had the copper by the time he reached the bakery.

The intended answer requires knowing whether and when the Ralph/Franklin swap was revealed to Osborne, but the chapter's own account of the Psalm trick never narrates a reveal, and the closest modern parallel example has the tester stay silent rather than reveal anything -- so no option is forced by the prose and the question cannot be fairly derived.

The 'Try this now' section claims the letter addressed to Basket, the king's printer, was the one that turned out to be from Riddlesden. But the Deep read and Card 5 both clearly state these were two different letters: the Basket letter was separate from the stationer's letter that turned out to be from Riddlesden (Card 5 even says the Basket letter 'was genuine'). This is a decidable, on-page contradiction about a fact the practical exercise itself depends on.

The full read is supposed to be a standalone depth option, but it introduces 'James Ralph' and refers to 'Denham himself' without ever identifying who they are within that section, relying on the reader having already read the fast/deep reads first.

Q1 asserts Coleman and Grace personally warned Franklin that Meredith was playing low games, but the Hook establishes they showed up only after word had already spread from elsewhere, and their actual on-page action was offering to cover the shop's cost, not delivering a warning.

The fast read first states Franklin picked thirteen virtues from the outset, then in the same paragraph says adding Humility after the Quaker friend's criticism 'made thirteen virtues in all,' implying the list only reached thirteen after that later addition. Both counts of the starting list size cannot be true at once, and this is decidable from this page alone.

The chapter names two different-sounding projects from the same May 19th, 1731 notes — 'Society of the Free and Easy' (Hook, Example 6, and the quiz's Q3 answer key) and 'United Party for Virtue' (Full read) — and attaches the identical defining fact (a thirteen-week practice requirement before admission) to both without ever clarifying whether these are one plan or two nested plans, leaving a careful reader unable to say what Franklin actually proposed or called it.

The distractor logic in options b and c is internally inconsistent, making the intended correct answer impossible to derive with confidence: option b implies that zero inoculation risk would disprove the friend's 'always safer' rule (the rule only requires inoculation to be lower-risk than disease, not risk-free, so this is backward), and option c's 'unless' condition requires the disease's risk to be 'similar to' inoculation's, which would undercut rather than support an 'always safer' claim.

The question requires judging when to refuse a blanket claim about inoculation's safety, but the chapter's only supporting material is one unelaborated sentence with no stated information about inoculation's own risk. The keyed answer depends on a comparison the page never supplies, while the literal anecdote (regret over skipping inoculation) actually points toward the rejected option, making the question unanswerable purely from the prose.

The Full read is presented as the deepest standalone layer but presumes facts and named specifics only introduced in the Deep read. It references 'his trick with the Assembly rival' and resolves it with a maxim without ever stating what the trick was (borrowing a book), so a reader who opens Full read without first reading Deep read cannot reconstruct the concrete action being praised.

The passage enumerates only silver dollars and gold pistoles as the money Franklin carried that night, then two sentences later has him give up copper coins first, even though copper was never established as being in his pocket.

A wording tell runs through the quiz: wrong options that use 'proof' or 'proves' are consistently incorrect, and no correct answer ever uses either word. In Q6 both wrong options contain 'proves,' so a reader can identify the correct option purely from that pattern without reading or reasoning about the chapter's content, undermining the quiz's validity as an assessment.

The fast read covers only the night-watch/fire-company thread and never mentions Whitefield at all, even though Whitefield's story is roughly half the chapter and is the subject basis for three quiz questions (Q3, Q5, Q9) and several review cards. A reader who consumes only the 'fast' layer gets a materially incomplete picture of the chapter, breaking the standalone promise of a layered fast/deep/full summary.

The chapter first says the lamp is publicly credited to John Clifton rather than Franklin ('An improved street lamp he refined is credited to a man named John Clifton, not to Franklin himself'), which is presented as an instance of Franklin declining credit for his own work. But the very next paragraph attributes the invention outright to Franklin without qualification ('Franklin's replacement used four flat panes...'), and a later reflection calls it 'Clifton's lamp idea' as though the idea itself, not just the public byline, belonged to Clifton. A reader cannot determine from the page whether the lamp was Franklin's invention that he assigned away, or genuinely Clifton's idea that Franklin merely refined, which undercuts the very 'he keeps handing the credit to someone else' claim the passage is making about itself.

The chapter gives two incompatible accounts of the same rejection vote. Deep read describes an in-session ambush where a member waited for Franklin to leave the room during a sitting. Example 4's tie-back instead says the vote was timed for a whole day when Franklin was already away, a premeditated calendar move rather than a spur-of-the-moment one. The Implementation plan's If-then 3 is built on the calendar-scheduling version, so the practical advice does not actually match the deep-read version of the event it claims to generalize from, and neither version is ever reconciled on the page.

Example 5's callback sentence claims the Sancho Panza dinner joke itself 'nearly cost Morris his post,' but the Deep read attributes his wearing-out-and-quitting to the returned pattern of official-message smearing, not to the private dinner joke, which the text frames as a friendly, in-group jab that never touched the friendship.

Card 3 asks readers to recall 'What made Franklin ask the Assembly for money to gift Dunbar's officers' as if this is established chapter content, but no such episode appears anywhere in the Fast read, Deep read, or Full read. A reader who studied only the reads (the card's stated source material) has no way to answer or even recognize this card, breaking its standalone/derivable promise.

The example's mechanism paragraph claims Patricia's deliberately undisclosed, untracked fix ('no debt gets tracked on either side') runs on 'that same plain logic' as Franklin's waggon deal. But the chapter's own account of Franklin's deal is the opposite of untracked: it was a printed, dated public offer secured by Franklin's own signed bond, which generated real, trackable liability (near-£20,000 in claims against him). Calling these 'the same plain logic' misstates the chapter's central mechanism within the page itself.

blockers.location: ch17/seat-skeptic/Deep read vs Review card 3 vs Quiz Q7
blockers.message: The Deep read attributes the rum-after-prayers fix to Franklin himself ('Franklin's fix was simple'), but Review card 3 attributes the identical action to the chaplain, Mr. Beatty, and Quiz Q7's keyed answer likewise assigns the move to the chaplain rather than Franklin, so the chapter disagrees with itself about who actually solved the attendance problem.

blockers.location: ch17/seat-practitioner/Deep read / Review Card 3 / Quiz Q7
blockers.message: The chapter attributes the decision to move rum distribution to right after prayers to Franklin in the Deep read, but to the chaplain in Review Card 3, and Quiz Q7's correct-reading option assumes it 'falls to the chaplain' to make the change. These three passages disagree about who owns this concrete decision, which also undermines the soundness of Q7's answer key.

The Hook flatly states Franklin never responded to Nollet in writing, but the Full read says he actually began writing a reply and only stopped short of sending it. These are two different claims about the same event, decidable from the page alone.

Card 6 asserts Nollet 'confirmed Franklin wrote the papers' and rejected the experiments anyway, while Quiz Q3 and Example 6 both frame Nollet as doubting that Franklin actually wrote the work. The chapter gives two incompatible accounts of Nollet's stance on authorship.

The Hook flatly states Franklin never replied to Nollet in writing, but the Full read says he drafted a reply and only withheld sending it — a direct factual conflict about whether any writing happened at all, and one that undercuts the chapter's own later instruction to 'draft it, then hold it unsent.'

The base narrative gives Nollet's motive as refusing to accept that an untrained American had beaten him to the discovery (a priority dispute), but Card 6 and Example 6 instead claim Nollet doubted Franklin's authorship of the papers and that Canton's replication of the pointed-rod experiment later 'confirmed' who wrote them — a claim about authorship that a physical replication cannot logically settle and that the rest of the page never supports.

Quiz Q3's premise says a Nollet-like rival 'refuses to believe you wrote your own work,' but Card 6 states the opposite: Nollet confirmed Franklin wrote the papers and rejected the findings anyway. The chapter's own review material contradicts the scenario its quiz question is built on.

The Full read introduces 'that dinner' and 'Denny's offer' with a definite article as if already established, then has Franklin refuse it, but no earlier section (Hook, Fast read, Deep read) nor the Full read itself ever explains what the dinner or offer was — that content only appears later in Example 2 and Example 4's connective paragraphs. A reader relying on the Full read as a standalone account hits an unexplained event.

The Full Read treats 'Denny's offer at that dinner' as already-established background and builds the causal chain on it, but no read layer (fast/deep/full) ever narrates what that offer was; the medal, the Madeira, and the request for a favor only appear later in Example 2 and Quiz Q4/Card 2, so the deepest summary fails its stand-alone promise.

Example 3 describes the Dutchman rescue and the shilling payment to the boatmen as happening on the same boat ride ('during a crossing... for his own passage'), but the chapter's own Deep read and Fast read separate these into two different legs of the journey: the Dutchman is saved on 'the boat crossing toward Amboy,' while the shilling is paid to 'the boatmen who had rowed him in' on the later leg that ends at the Philadelphia market where he buys bread.

blockers.location: ch03/seat-skeptic/Full read / Key takeaway / Try this now / Implementation plan
blockers.message: The chapter explicitly denies there is one unifying lesson ('No single trick explains a life built from many small recoveries'), yet it simultaneously offers three different, non-overlapping single-skill claims as the chapter's takeaway: exact record-keeping (Key takeaway), giving a specific referral (Try this now), and testing a named second opinion (Implementation plan Core skill), with no reconciliation of which one is 'the' lesson.

The section's own Core skill (get a named second opinion and test it with a small real task before committing) is never instantiated by any of its three If-then rules: If-then 1 is about referring someone else outward, If-then 2 is about repaying a declined favor, and If-then 3 is about repairing a bad first impression through repeated exposure. A reader following the If-thens would not be practicing the stated Core skill at all, breaking the section's own stand-alone promise.

The quiz stem asserts Franklin's condition for joining Keimer's sect was that Keimer 'also give up keeping the Seventh day, Sabbath,' but the Fast read and Deep read both establish the opposite: Franklin said he would allow the beard and Sabbath-keeping, and his actual condition was that Keimer give up meat. The keyed answer (b) repeats the same reversed claim about 'Sabbath doctrines.'

The chapter explicitly disclaims that Ralph's and Osborne's later-life outcomes prove anything about the earlier test, yet the quiz's only defensible answer requires readers to use those exact later outcomes (finished prose, career change) as the proof of 'talent' — the quiz's reasoning contradicts the narrative's own stated limit on the same page.

The Full read is presented as a standalone summary layer, but its closing sentences use a bare pronoun with no antecedent introduced anywhere in that section (Meredith is never named in Full read; he only appears in Deep read). A reader of Full read alone has no way to resolve 'He,' and the only same-section candidate (Keimer) directly conflicts with that section's own earlier account of Keimer and Franklin parting through a shouted quarrel, not a mutually agreed written settlement.

The card's Front asks a specific factual question (which habit resisted every fix) but the Back never names the answer (Order), instead pivoting to generic transfer advice, so the card fails its stand-alone promise to answer its own Front.

Full read is presented as one of three layered but standalone summaries, yet it repeatedly leans on named events and pronoun antecedents it never defines within itself, so a reader who starts at Full read (a plausible entry point given the stated layering) cannot follow it. It opens with an undefined 'this,' then later refers to 'The Charleston story' and 'The Hemphill affair' as if the reader already knows those episodes from Deep read.

The full read is supposed to be the deepest, standalone summary tier, but it repeatedly refers back to people and events (the widow, 'the Charleston story,' 'the Hemphill affair,' 'a hostile Assembly member') without reintroducing who they are or what happened, so it only makes sense to someone who already read the deep read. This fails the stand-alone promise the summaries factor requires.

The chapter's own practical example endorses deliberately mislabeling a bylaw-restricted purchase to a governing board and keeping a private 'true use' memo apart from the official minutes so the record won't contradict the cover story. A real reader (e.g., an actual condo treasurer) who follows this could expose themselves to breach-of-fiduciary-duty or fraud liability, and the chapter presents it as an unqualified win with no caveat about that risk.

Full read introduces 'the small sweeping subscription for the market street' as if it were already established, but no earlier section ever says the Craven-street paid trial became a subscription for a street called 'market street.' A reader relying on Full read (or even Deep read) alone cannot bridge this gap, breaking the section's stand-alone promise.

The quiz stem restates the Carlisle gathering as 'close to one hundred men,' dropping the women and children the chapter itself says were present, contradicting the chapter's own earlier description of the same event.

Example 1 claims the sect-balanced trustee structure governed 'the academy's building board... before its schools opened, in 1749,' but the Full read describes that same one-per-sect trustee makeup as belonging to the separate Whitefield building the school moved into only after it had already grown and needed a bigger home -- i.e., after the 1749 opening -- and as a different body from the subscription's own twenty-four trustees.

The Hook claims a committee compared 'four rival plans,' but no other section gives this count — the Deep read and Example 5 describe an unspecified/plural number of rival drafts, and every other 'four' in the chapter refers only to the four Pennsylvania commissioners, leaving an unresolved numeric conflict.

Deep read opens mid-story ('that spring') and never restates the year or the war-with-France motive established only in Fast read, so a reader entering at Deep read lacks basic who/when/why context, breaking the section's stand-alone promise.

Full read analyzes 'the plan' and 'the draft' at length but never states what the plan actually proposed (crown-picked president-general, colony-picked grand council); that structural fact only appears in Fast read and 'Try this now,' so Full read cannot stand alone for a reader who hasn't already read the earlier sections.

blockers.location: ch15/seat-practitioner/Example 2 (Lorraine's First Day on the Docket)
blockers.message: Example 2's closing paragraph claims Morris's veto 'ran on the same mechanism' as an exemption that becomes policy by accident, 'not because anyone decided it should but because repeating it is easier than questioning it.' This directly contradicts the Full read's own account that the exemption was a deliberate, explicit requirement the Penn family wrote into every governor's bond from the start.

Example 5 states 'neither man read the joke as anything but table talk,' but the Deep read explicitly says Franklin's retort in that same exchange 'was a jab at Morris's own habit of smearing the Assembly's name in his official messages' — i.e. it carried real pointed meaning tied to the public conflict, not mere banter.

The Deep read states 63 of 86 officers fell in the ambush, but Example 5 later describes the same event as the column having 'lost eighty-six officers,' implying total officer losses rather than 63 of 86. A reader comparing the two figures encounters a direct numeric conflict.

Example 4's takeaway instructs readers to surface problems visibly the instant they're spotted, while Example 6's takeaway instructs the opposite: quietly fix a colleague's error and never disclose it to anyone, including the person in charge. Both are presented as equally valid transferable lessons from the same chapter without reconciling the conflict.

The bolded, generalized takeaway tells readers to secretly fix another worker's error and tell no one, including the worker or supervisor, in a scenario explicitly about safety-relevant craftsmanship (rope for hoisting). Followed literally, this hides information a supervisor needs to catch a systemic training gap and lets a colleague be falsely credited for uncorrected work.

Full read references 'Franklin's warning about the marching line' as already-established, but that detail is introduced only in Deep read and is never defined within Full read itself, so a reader who lands only on Full read cannot follow the reference — breaking the chapter's own fast/deep/full standalone design.

Example 1's stated principle explicitly rejects folding corrections in silently, while Example 6's stated principle explicitly instructs fixing another person's error silently and never disclosing it. The two 'lessons' directly oppose each other on the same behavior (visibility vs. concealment of a fix), decidable from the page alone.

The Full read references 'the Bethlehem scene' and 'the forts' with a definite article as though already established, but Full read never itself introduces Bethlehem as a location or fort-building as an event — those facts exist only in the Fast read and Deep read above it. A reader who reads only the Full read tier (the promised deepest standalone layer) cannot tell what location or structures are being discussed.

blockers.location: ch18/seat-cold/deep read vs. full read (account of the mocked lightning paper's survival)
blockers.message: The deep read claims the paper 'survived only because two other men judged it worth printing,' but the full read (and the rest of the chapter) names only one rescuer, Dr. Fothergill, and even calls him 'that second reader' in the singular, never identifying a second man. The headcount of who saved the paper is inconsistent within the chapter itself.

blockers.location: ch18/seat-skeptic/Deep read vs. Full read vs. Card 2
blockers.message: Deep read states the mocked lightning paper 'survived only because two other men judged it worth printing,' but Full read and Card 2 attribute the entire save to one person, Dr. Fothergill, explicitly calling him 'that second reader' (singular). The chapter gives two incompatible headcounts for the same rescue.

blockers.location: ch18/seat-practitioner/Deep read vs. Full read (account of the lightning paper's survival)
blockers.message: Deep read claims the mocked lightning/electricity paper 'survived only because two other men judged it worth printing,' but the Full read's account of the same event names only one person, Dr. Fothergill, taking that action and explicitly calls him 'that second reader' (singular). No second name is ever given for this event anywhere on the page, so the count of rescuers is internally inconsistent.

The passage introduces exactly one uncle and one grandfather by name, then refers to them together as 'Two grandparents,' contradicting its own earlier identification of one of the two as an uncle rather than a grandparent.

The passage asserts 'Two grandparents showed Franklin something important' about putting a firm opinion in writing under one's own name, but the only person shown doing that in the surrounding text is Peter Folger, a single grandparent. The other example given right before it is Franklin's uncle Benjamin, who is not a grandparent, so the 'two grandparents' claim is not supported by, and conflicts with, the family relationships stated on the same page.

The chapter gives two incompatible explanations for why Franklin revealed himself as the anonymous essay's author: Full read frames it as a deliberate, patient move made once the verdict on the writing was already locked in, while Card 5 frames the same moment as an involuntary lapse caused by vanity overwhelming restraint.

Card 3's answer asserts a specific claim (that Benjamin was formally questioned by the council and only admonished) that is never introduced anywhere in the Fast, Deep, or Full read, so a reader who has only the chapter cannot verify, derive, or even recall this from what was taught. This breaks a review card's job of reinforcing content the chapter actually covered.

The fast read establishes that Franklin gave his copper coin to the boatmen before reaching the market, leaving only the dollar by the time he bought bread, but the quiz's own correct-answer text asserts he 'still had a Dutch dollar and copper coin' at that point, contradicting the chapter's own established sequence of events.

blockers.location: ch04/seat-practitioner/Try this now (vs. Deep read and Full read)
blockers.message: Try this now compresses the story so that Keith's specific promise to 'personally bankroll his own printing house' occurs during the initial street-crossing/Madeira scene at Keimer's shop. But Deep read explicitly dates that exact promise ('he would pay for the print shop himself') as a later, bigger escalation made only after Franklin's father refused, and Full read explicitly says the street-crossing visit itself 'guaranteed nothing on its own' and was 'just an opening move' with no promise attached.

blockers.location: ch05/seat-skeptic/Implementation plan (Core skill) vs. Deep read / Q4
blockers.message: The chapter's entire modeled method treats a single unwatched catch as sufficient proof (Keimer's one lapse ends the diet test; Q4's correct answer says one instance of eating alone, not ordering, is the evidence), but the Implementation Plan's Core skill instructs readers to withhold judgment until they have logged forty separate instances before calling any pattern proven, directly contradicting the one-catch standard taught everywhere else on the page.

The Deep read and Full read each open by referencing 'Keimer' and the diet bargain as already-established facts, never (re)introducing who Keimer is or what the bargain was. A reader who opens directly to Deep or Full — a normal workflow in a layered fast/deep/full format — starts confused about the premise, breaking the standalone promise for two of the three read tiers.

The chapter states the notebook 'gave each virtue its own page' and then, in the same passage, describes a single page carrying rows for all thirteen virtues, directly contradicting the claim that each virtue had a separate page.
Example 6's closing explanation asserts a much larger and more specific fallout from the Hemphill plagiarism than the chapter's own Full read states elsewhere on the same page.

The if-then explicitly warns against moving a demonstration quietly without posting a notice, but the narrative it is drawn from shows Carmen doing exactly that with no notice posted, and it still draws the largest crowd the demonstration ever had, contradicting the lesson's own premise.

The story shows Nora making a single quiet, private refund out of her own purse to two widows, yet the closing paragraph claims she established 'a habit of publishing the true figure' that became a standing rule the club still follows, a publishing habit the narrative never depicts.

blockers.location: ch12/seat-cold/Review cards, Card 7 vs Deep read
blockers.message: Card 7's answer justifies the lottery by claiming that without it, one pool would have been 'responsible for both signatures and cannon' — implying cannon costs were something the pledge/lottery funds needed to cover. But the Deep read explicitly states pledge money 'could not buy cannon' at all, and that every cannon came from an external loan negotiated with Governor Clinton in New York, never from the lottery or pledge funds. The card's own stated rationale misdescribes what the chapter elsewhere says the lottery and pledge money did and did not fund.

The chapter gives two incompatible sequences for the stove-patent event. Deep read frames Franklin as actively declining an already-offered patent, implying a live choice at the moment of the offer. Example 6 states the design was given away before any patent was ever offered, making the later offer moot rather than actively refused. A reader cannot tell which chronology is accurate from the page.

blockers.location: ch12/seat-practitioner/Example 3: Five to One Before the Rain
blockers.message: The example's title implies a 5-1 vote (echoing the chapter's own 8-to-1 fire-company margin it explicitly calls back to), but the vote it actually describes is three in favor, one opposed (3-1); none of the example's stated numbers (seven members, six others, three absent) combine to produce five, so the title contradicts the body's own tally.

The full read references 'Bond' and 'the hospital plan' as if already known, but that context (Dr. Thomas Bond, the stalled hospital fundraising) is only established in the deep read. A reader who lands on full read without the deep read cannot follow the line, breaking the section's stand-alone promise.

The Fast read tells a reader that 'two courts said no,' but no court of law is ever involved anywhere in the chapter; the Deep and Full reads consistently identify the two rejecting bodies as the colonial assemblies (a legislature) and the Board of Trade (an administrative board). A reader who only reads the Fast read comes away with a materially wrong picture of what kind of bodies rejected the plan, which breaks the standalone-accuracy promise a summary layer is supposed to keep.

Unlike Fast read and Deep read, which each restate the year, location, and reason for the trip, Full read opens directly into analysis and later references 'this errand' without ever re-establishing what happened, breaking the stated design promise that each summary layer stands alone.

Fast read covers only the waggon-procurement half of the chapter and never mentions Braddock's ambush, Dunbar's collapse, or Braddock's scorn for warnings/scouts. But the Key takeaway states both halves as the chapter's core lesson. A reader who only reads Fast read (the intended quick layer) ends up with a takeaway that references content they never saw, breaking the standalone promise of the fast summary.

blockers.location: ch18/seat-skeptic/Full read vs. Quiz Q3 stem / Example 6 bridge paragraph
blockers.message: The chapter's own narrative (Full read) says Nollet's objection was that he 'could not accept that an untrained American had beaten him to the discovery' — a dispute over scientific priority/credibility. Two other sections invent a different, more specific claim not supported anywhere in the narrative: that Nollet doubted Franklin literally wrote his own papers (a claim about authorship/authenticity, not priority). A careful reader who checks the quiz stem or Example 6 against the Full read will find the underlying fact restated inconsistently.

Example 3's tie-back claims Loudoun's army 'idled outside Louisburg,' but the Full read explicitly locates the stalled campaign's drills at Halifax and states he returned without ever conducting a siege, contradicting the claim that the army was stationed outside Louisbourg itself.

Card 6 states the ministry ('tithe-son') plan 'gave way to' grammar school, implying grammar school came as a replacement after the ministry plan ended. The Full read establishes the opposite sequence: grammar school was pursued AS PART OF the ministry plan ('Grammar school seemed to prove the plan right') and both the schooling and the ministry aspiration ended together because of cost.

'Old Bradford' is introduced two sentences after 'Andrew Bradford' with no signal that this is a different person (Andrew's father); a first-time reader is likely to read him as the same Bradford who just refused Franklin work, and the only disambiguating clue is an indirect later clause ('his rival's own father') that requires inference to resolve. This leaves the standalone Deep-read layer momentarily incoherent on a load-bearing plot point.

The Fast read states Vernon directly handed Franklin the money to carry, but Quiz Q3's setup describes a different mechanism: Franklin being asked to go collect a debt owed to Vernon from someone in a town he's passing through. These are two incompatible accounts of how Franklin obtained the same sum, decidable purely by comparing the two passages on the page.

The fast read describes Vernon as 'a stranger's friend' who personally handed Franklin the money to carry south, but Q3's stem recasts him as 'a friend of your brother's' who asks Franklin to go collect a debt owed to him in a town he's passing through — a different relationship and a different transaction than the one the narrative describes.

The Key takeaway groups the Miss Read courtship with the diet and byline bargains as the same kind of 'test' that shows 'what someone truly believed,' directly contradicting the Full read's explicit statement that the courtship was 'not a test of character' and its warning against 'folding every relationship into one shape.'

Every card's 'Back:' line is preceded by roughly ten leading spaces after the line break, which exceeds the 4-space threshold that triggers an indented code block under standard Markdown/CommonMark rendering, risking the answer text displaying as raw monospaced code instead of normal prose in the app.

blockers.location: ch06/seat-cold/deep read vs. Example 3 vs. Review card 1
blockers.message: The chapter gives three incompatible accounts of how many pressmen adopted Franklin's water-drinking breakfast: the deep read says only a few did, while an example and a review card both claim the whole shop of fifty did, undercutting the 'quiet example over mandate' lesson those very sections are built to teach.

The deep read states categorically that Keith never wrote any of the letters in the mail bag, but Review card 5 asserts one of those same two letters (to Basket) 'was genuine,' directly contradicting the chapter's own account of the central plot fact the reveal depends on.

Example 5 attributes the fraudulent/disputed letter to 'Basket's print shop,' but the deep read explicitly separates the two mailbag letters: one genuinely addressed to Basket, and a separate, unnamed stationer's letter that turned out to be from Riddlesden. The example's closing line still credits 'a London stationer' (not Basket) with catching the forgery, so the example's own setup contradicts its own payoff and the source anecdote it claims to mirror.

Every other section establishes Watts's as the only print shop Franklin worked at ('Franklin laid down his composing stick at Watts's printing house', 'At Watts's shop, the compositors asked him...'), then the full read suddenly has him 'setting its type at Palmer's' with no introduction of a second shop or transition between them, breaking the full read's promise to stand alone and be comprehensible on its own terms.

blockers.location: ch08/seat-skeptic/Fast read / Full read / Implementation plan / Quiz Q1
blockers.message: The chapter gives two incompatible explanations for why currency grew from 15,000 to 80,000 pounds without lasting complaint. Fast read and the Implementation plan credit the uncontested pamphlet itself for the sustained growth/acceptance, while Full read, Card 6, Example 6, and the quiz's own designated correct answer (Q1a) instead credit ongoing trade, building, and population growth. A reader who trusts the Fast read is set up to pick the answer the quiz marks wrong.

The Deep read's opening line presupposes the Fast read's content ('the same trick') without defining the trick within the Deep read itself, so the section fails its standalone-read promise if a reader lands here first.

The full read is meant to stand alone but presupposes unexplained context from the deep read: it references 'the funding trick' for the hospital and 'a subscription for the academy' without ever restating what the trick or subscription was within the full read itself, so a reader who starts at full read cannot follow these references.

Deep read opens with an undefined reference to a fix never explained in that section, and Full read — nominally the most complete version — never states the actual waggon-hire terms (fifteen shillings per diem, upfront pay, lost-horse pay) that are the chapter's central technique.
